warmup.q: A Quarkus 3 service written in Kotlin has a bean annotated @jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped, and no compiler plugins. What does javap show for the class?
options: public class: CDI annotations make a class open
public final class: Kotlin classes are final unless something opens them
It depends on the JDK version
The class doesn't compile until you add open
warmup.why: Kotlin makes classes and their members final by default, and an annotation is just data: it doesn't change modifiers unless a compiler plugin reads it. That's what all-open is for. Quarkus can sometimes work around final classes at build time, but the class file itself is final. Many people expect the first option because Java classes are open by default.

sections.h: Kotlin classes are final, and framework proxies need to subclass them
sections.html:
Quarkus, Spring and Hibernate add behavior to your classes with proxies: classes they generate that extend yours and override each method, to do something before and after calling super. A @Transactional method gets an overriding method that opens a transaction, calls yours and commits. Write such a subclass by hand and the problem shows at once:

Java
class AuditedSettlementService extends SettlementService {   // error: cannot inherit from final SettlementService
    @Override public String settle(String batch) { return super.settle(batch); }
}
Kotlin
class TimedSettlementService : SettlementService() {          // error: this type is final, so it cannot be extended.
    override fun settle(batch: String): String =                // error: 'settle' in 'SettlementService' is final
        super.settle(batch)                                     //        and cannot be overridden.
}

Kotlin classes and their members are final unless you write open. A framework that generates subclasses hits the same wall as your hand-written one, just later. You could write open on every bean and every method, and nobody keeps that up.

A compiler plugin is a jar that the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it emits. The all-open plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword", for every class that carries an annotation you configure (or whose superclass does, or that uses a meta-annotation built on it). This lab module configures it for workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies. javap on the demo's SettlementService then shows public class and public java.lang.String settle(...), with no final. What it leaves alone is just as important: private members stay private, backing fields stay private final, and an unannotated PlainHelper stays public final class.

kotlin-spring is all-open with a preset for Spring's annotations, such as @Component and @Transactional. Quarkus users need care. The quarkus preset inside the Kotlin 2.4.21 plugin lists only javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped and RequestScoped, but Quarkus 3 uses the jakarta namespace. In a test run, a jakarta-annotated bean compiled with that preset stayed public final class. Name the annotations yourself, as the Quarkus Kotlin guide does for jakarta.ws.rs.Path and jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped:

// build.gradle.kts of a Quarkus 3 service
plugins {
    kotlin("plugin.allopen") version "2.4.21"
}

allOpen {
    annotation("jakarta.ws.rs.Path")
    annotation("jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped")
}

Quarkus's CDI container can also transform many final classes at build time (quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default), but its Kotlin guide still configures all-open, and so should you.

try.title: Open a class without writing open
steps: Run AllOpenDemo, then AllOpenDemoJava, which extends the same Kotlin class from Java.
Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SettlementService from labs/. Which members are still final?
Delete @OpenForProxies above SettlementService. Predict the errors, run, and put it back.

code.title: AllOpenDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies import java.lang.reflect.Modifier /** Marked for all-open: the plugin makes the class and its members open at compile time. */ @OpenForProxies class SettlementService { val feeBps: Int = 125 fun settle(batch: String): String = "settled $batch at $feeBps bps" private fun secret(): Int = 42 // private stays private, and final } /** Not marked: final, like every Kotlin class by default. */ class PlainHelper { fun help(): String = "help" } /** What a framework generates at build or run time: a subclass that wraps every call. */ class TimedSettlementService : SettlementService() { override fun settle(batch: String): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return super.settle(batch) } finally { println(" settle took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } } fun describe(cls: Class<*>) { val methods = cls.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.joinToString { m -> val kind = when { Modifier.isPrivate(m.modifiers) -> "private" Modifier.isFinal(m.modifiers) -> "final" else -> "open" } "${m.name}:$kind" } println("${cls.simpleName}: ${if (Modifier.isFinal(cls.modifiers)) "final" else "open"} class; $methods") } fun main() { describe(SettlementService::class.java) describe(PlainHelper::class.java) val service: SettlementService = TimedSettlementService() println(service.settle("batch-17")) // Wrong move. Delete @OpenForProxies above SettlementService, predict, run. }

alt.title: AllOpenDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of AllOpenDemo.kt. Java classes are open unless you write final, so Java can extend the * Kotlin class only because all-open removed its final. Remove the marker and javac says: * "cannot inherit from final SettlementService". */ public class AllOpenDemoJava { static final class AuditedSettlementService extends SettlementService { @Override public String settle(String batch) { System.out.println(" audit: settling " + batch); return super.settle(batch); } } public static void main(String[] args) { SettlementService service = new AuditedSettlementService(); System.out.println(service.settle("batch-17")); AllOpenDemoKt.describe(PlainHelper.class); } }

try.expect: The demo prints SettlementService: open class; getFeeBps:open, secret:private, settle:open, PlainHelper: final class; help:final, a timing line and settled batch-17 at 125 bps. javap shows public class SettlementService, private final int feeBps and private int secret(): only the field keeps its final. Without the marker, the build fails with this type is final, so it cannot be extended. and 'settle' in 'SettlementService' is final and cannot be overridden., and the Java twin would get cannot inherit from final SettlementService.

sections.h: no-arg gives frameworks an empty constructor, and skips your initializers
sections.html:
Hibernate builds an entity the same way every time: call a constructor with no parameters, then set the fields from the row. Its documentation says an entity must "be a non-final class, with a non-private constructor with no parameters". A Kotlin class like LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) has no such constructor. By hand, you'd add one:

Java
@Entity
public class LedgerRow {
    @Id private String id;
    private long amountMinor;
    private String note = "default-note";

    protected LedgerRow() { }                       // for Hibernate
    public LedgerRow(String id, long amountMinor) { this.id = id; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; }
}
Kotlin
class LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) {
    var note: String = "default-note"

    constructor() : this("", 0)                    // the hand-written version: invented defaults
}

The hand-written Kotlin constructor works, but it invents an empty id that any Kotlin caller can now create by mistake. The no-arg plugin generates the constructor for classes with an annotation you configure, and the docs say it's "annotated with @Deprecated at the HIDDEN level, so you can call it from Java but not from Kotlin". The demo shows both sides: Kotlin's LedgerRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'., and Java's new LedgerRow() compiles, with only a deprecation note from javac.

Now the trap. The generated constructor doesn't run property initializers. The option that would run them, invokeInitializers, is "disabled by default". So after new LedgerRow(), note holds null, even though Kotlin declared it a non-null String, and the first note.length in Kotlin code throws a NullPointerException. For a JPA entity that's usually fine, because Hibernate sets every mapped column right afterwards. For anything else, turn invokeInitializers on or give the property no initializer.

For JPA, use kotlin-jpa rather than configuring no-arg yourself: it's no-arg with a preset for @Entity, @Embeddable and @MappedSuperclass, in both the javax.persistence and jakarta.persistence packages. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, the Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin also applies all-open with the JPA preset, so that, in the release notes' words, "lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading". On older Kotlin versions you had to add all-open for entities yourself.

try.title: Build an entity the way an ORM does
steps: Run NoArgDemo, then NoArgDemoJava. Predict blank.note before you look.
Uncomment the wrong move in NoArgDemo.kt, predict, run, and comment it out again.
In NoArgDemo.kt, add println(blank.note.length) at the end of main. Predict what happens, then run.

code.title: NoArgDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity /** no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor that only Java and reflection can call. */ @NoArgEntity class LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) { var note: String = "default-note" } fun main() { // the way an ORM builds an empty entity before it fills in the columns val blank = LedgerRow::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println("blank.amountMinor = ${blank.amountMinor}") println("blank.note is null: ${(blank.note as String?) == null}") // declared String, holds null println("normal note = ${LedgerRow("row-1", 100).note}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // val direct = LedgerRow() }

alt.title: NoArgDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of NoArgDemo.kt. Java can call the generated constructor directly: it is hidden from * Kotlin with @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN), which javac doesn't enforce. */ public class NoArgDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { LedgerRow blank = new LedgerRow(); // compiles in Java System.out.println("blank.amountMinor = " + blank.getAmountMinor()); System.out.println("blank.note = " + blank.getNote()); // null: the initializer never ran System.out.println("blank.getId() = " + blank.getId()); } }

The Kotlin call LedgerRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'. and the same for amountMinor. The added line compiles, because note is declared String, and throws NullPointerException at run time.

sections.h: kotlinx.serialization writes the serializer at compile time
sections.html:
Most JSON libraries on the JVM work by reflection: at run time they look at a class, find its constructor and properties, and guess how to fill them. Kotlin classes make that guessing harder, with default arguments and non-null types. kotlinx.serialization doesn't guess. "When you annotate a class with @Serializable, the Kotlin serialization plugin generates a KSerializer for that class." The demo's Posted gets a nested class, Posted$$serializer, that implements GeneratedSerializer<Posted> with real serialize and deserialize methods, plus Posted.serializer() on the companion object. Without the plugin, Posted.serializer() is unresolved reference 'serializer'.

Java
// Java's usual approach, with Jackson: annotations read by reflection at run time
@JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type")
@JsonSubTypes({
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Posted.class, name = "posted"),
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Reversed.class, name = "reversed")
})
public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed { String paymentId(); }

String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(events);
Kotlin
@Serializable
sealed interface LedgerEvent { val paymentId: String }

@Serializable @SerialName("posted")
data class Posted(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String = "EUR") : LedgerEvent

@Serializable @SerialName("reversed")
data class Reversed(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String? = null) : LedgerEvent

private val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false }
val text = json.encodeToString(events)      // events: List<LedgerEvent>

A sealed hierarchy is "closed polymorphism": the plugin knows every subclass at compile time, so it can write and read a "type" field, the class discriminator that tells a decoder which subclass an object is, with no registration. Three details decide what the JSON looks like. The discriminator is written only when the static type is the base: List<LedgerEvent> gets "type":"posted", and Json.encodeToString(p) with p typed Posted gets none. Its value is the fully qualified class name unless you set @SerialName, so without it a package rename changes your wire format. And the default Json leaves out properties that equal their default (encodeDefaults is off), writes nulls, and rejects unknown keys: Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer'.

For events that cross a Kafka topic, that last default matters most. A consumer with the default Json breaks the day a producer adds a field, so set ignoreUnknownKeys = true. Build one Json instance and reuse it: the docs say instances "are immutable and thread-safe", and that reusing them improves performance. The JSON format is Stable; HOCON, ProtoBuf, CBOR and Properties are still Experimental.

try.title: Read the JSON a sealed hierarchy produces
steps: Run SerializationDemo. Before you do, predict which lines will contain "type".
Remove @SerialName("posted") from Posted and run again. What is the type value now?
Run SerializationDemoJava, which uses the generated serializer from Java through Posted.Companion.serializer().

code.title: SerializationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName import kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json @Serializable sealed interface LedgerEvent { val paymentId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("posted") data class Posted(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String = "EUR") : LedgerEvent @Serializable @SerialName("reversed") data class Reversed(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String? = null) : LedgerEvent private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } fun main() { val events: List<LedgerEvent> = listOf(Posted("pay_1", 1_999), Reversed("pay_1")) val text = lenient.encodeToString(events) println(text) println("round trip equal: ${lenient.decodeFromString<List<LedgerEvent>>(text) == events}") val p = Posted("pay_2", 1) println("static type Posted: ${Json.encodeToString(p)}") println("static type LedgerEvent: ${Json.encodeToString<LedgerEvent>(p)}") val newer = """{"type":"posted","paymentId":"pay_3","amountMinor":5,"acquirer":"acq-a"}""" println("lenient: ${lenient.decodeFromString<LedgerEvent>(newer)}") try { Json.decodeFromString<LedgerEvent>(newer) } catch (e: SerializationException) { println("default Json: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}") } println("generated serializer: ${Posted.serializer().javaClass.name}") }

alt.title: SerializationDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json; /** * Java twin of SerializationDemo.kt. The plugin's output is ordinary bytecode, so Java can use it: * Posted.Companion.serializer() returns the generated KSerializer, and Json.Default does the rest. * Java code normally uses Jackson instead; this shows what the plugin generated. */ public class SerializationDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Posted p = new Posted("pay_2", 1L, "EUR"); String text = Json.Default.encodeToString(Posted.Companion.serializer(), p); System.out.println("Java, static type Posted: " + text); Posted back = Json.Default.decodeFromString(Posted.Companion.serializer(), text); System.out.println("decoded: " + back + ", equal: " + back.equals(p)); System.out.println("generated serializer: " + Posted.Companion.serializer().getClass().getName()); } }

try.expect: The list prints [{"type":"posted","paymentId":"pay_1","amountMinor":1999},{"type":"reversed","paymentId":"pay_1"}]: no currency (it equals its default) and no reason (null, with explicitNulls = false). The static-type Posted line has no type; the LedgerEvent line has one. The lenient instance ignores acquirer, and the default one fails with Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer'. Without @SerialName the type becomes workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.Posted. The Java twin prints the same JSON and the class name Posted$$serializer.

sections.h: KSP and kapt generate new source files instead
sections.html:
The three plugins above change the compiler's output from the inside. A second family of tools generates new source files from your annotations, the way Java annotation processors do: dependency injection (Dagger), database access (Room), mappers (MapStruct).

kapt runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". Those stubs are Java declarations of your Kotlin classes, written only so a Java processor can read them, and the migration guide calls them "expensive": they "significantly increase build time" and lose Kotlin-specific features. KSP is the Kotlin-native alternative, "a source code generation framework for Kotlin". Its processors read Kotlin declarations directly, and its README says they "can run up to 2x faster" than kapt. The limits are part of the design: KSP processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code". They only add new files.

Two version facts matter in 2026. KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin" and is built on the same compiler APIs as IntelliJ IDEA. And since KSP 2.3.0, KSP1 is deprecated and "KSP version is no longer tied to the Kotlin compiler version", so a KSP release number no longer has to match your Kotlin version.

My rule: use KSP whenever the library ships a KSP processor, and kapt only for processors that exist just for Java. Keep an eye on build time when you add kapt: every kapt module pays for the stub step on each build.

A check to end on, and the answer follows from how the serialization plugin works: a module depends on the kotlinx-serialization-json library but doesn't apply kotlin("plugin.serialization"). You mark a class @Serializable and call Captured.serializer(). What happens, and at which stage? (It fails at compile time with unresolved reference 'serializer'.: the annotation compiles because it's in the library, but nobody generates the companion function.)

analogy: Compiler plugins are the print shop's finishing step. Your manuscript says "open for proxies" or "needs a blank form" in the margin, and the finisher acts on the note: it trims the final off, binds in an extra blank page (the no-arg constructor), or prints a matching order form for each document (the serializer). The reader of the finished book, the JVM, only sees the result. The analogy breaks with the blank page: a real finisher wouldn't hand you a form with required fields left empty, but no-arg does exactly that, which is why the initializer trap exists.
world: A Quarkus 3 payment service in Kotlin needs all three. All-open, configured with the jakarta annotations by name (jakarta.ws.rs.Path, jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped), so ArC and RESTEasy can subclass your beans and resources; don't trust a preset that knows only javax. kotlin-jpa for Hibernate entities, which on Kotlin 2.3.20 and later also opens them for lazy-loading proxies. And kotlinx.serialization for the PaymentEvent messages on your Kafka topics, with a @SerialName on every subtype so a package rename can't break consumers, and ignoreUnknownKeys = true so a producer can add a field without taking down every consumer.
mistake:
Relying on a preset that doesn't match your annotations, and finding out from a proxy error at startup or, worse, from interceptors that silently don't run. With Kotlin 2.4.21 the all-open plugin's quarkus preset knows only javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped and RequestScoped, while Quarkus 3 code uses jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped:

Java
// in Java the question doesn't exist: classes are open unless you write final
@ApplicationScoped
public class FeeService { public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * 125 / 10_000; } }
Kotlin
@ApplicationScoped              // jakarta.enterprise.context: not in the 2.4.21 quarkus preset
class FeeService {              // javap: public final class FeeService
    fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * 125 / 10_000
}

The fix is to list the annotations you use, with their full jakarta names, in allOpen { annotation(...) }, and to check one bean with javap after any build change.

compare.title: A proxy-ready service and entity: Java as written vs Kotlin with plugins

java.title: Beans.java
java.html: @ApplicationScoped public class FeeService { // open by default in Java public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * 125 / 10_000; } } @Entity public class PaymentEntity { // open by default @Id private String id; private long amountMinor; private String note = "default-note"; // runs in every constructor protected PaymentEntity() { } // the no-arg constructor, written by hand public PaymentEntity(String id, long amountMinor) { this.id = id; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } }

kotlin.title: Beans.kt
kotlin.html: @ApplicationScoped // all-open configured for this annotation class FeeService { fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * 125 / 10_000 } @Entity // kotlin-jpa: no-arg + all-open for entities class PaymentEntity(@Id val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) { var note: String = "default-note" // skipped by the generated no-arg constructor }

compare.note: Java gets proxy-ready classes for free: classes and methods are open unless marked final, and you write the no-arg constructor yourself, where field initializers run as usual. Kotlin's defaults point the other way, so the plugins put back what frameworks need, at compile time, driven by annotations. The class files end up close to the Java ones, with one difference that bites: Kotlin's generated no-arg constructor skips property initializers unless you enable invokeInitializers, so note is null on a fresh instance, while Java's hand-written constructor runs note = "default-note".

worked.title: Version a Kafka event without breaking consumers

steps.say: Version 1 of a payment event goes onto a topic. The consumer uses the default Json. Here are both sides, with the Java consumer using Jackson.
steps.code: // Java consumer with Jackson: by default it also fails on unknown properties ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper(); Captured c = mapper.readValue(record.value(), Captured.class);

alt.html: @Serializable @SerialName("captured") data class Captured(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent val event = Json.decodeFromString<PaymentEvent>(record.value()) // the default Json: strict

steps.say: The producer team adds acquirer and deploys first. Every consumer with the default settings now fails on every message, because unknown keys "result in an error" by default.
steps.code: // producer v2 writes {"type":"captured","paymentId":"pay_7","amountMinor":1999,"acquirer":"acq-a"} Json.decodeFromString<PaymentEvent>(v2) // SerializationException: ... Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer' at path: $

alt.html: mapper.readValue(v2, Captured.class); // Jackson: UnrecognizedPropertyException, unless FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is turned off

steps.say: Configure the consumer once, in one shared instance: tolerate new keys, keep @SerialName stable, and add new fields with defaults so old messages still decode.
steps.code: // 1. one instance, reused: immutable and thread-safe val events = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } // 2. a new field gets a default, so v1 messages without it still decode @Serializable @SerialName("captured") data class Captured(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val acquirer: String? = null) : PaymentEvent

alt.html: ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper() .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);

steps.say: Check the other direction. A v1 consumer that doesn't know a new subtype, say "type":"chargeback", still fails, and it should: ignoreUnknownKeys covers fields, not types. Deploy consumers before producers when you add a subtype.

lab.title: A serializable event hierarchy and proxy-ready classes
steps: Read Annotations.kt and the two plugin lines in labs/kotlin/build.gradle.kts. The annotations do nothing by themselves; the plugins look for their names.
Run the tests. All seven fail.
In PaymentEvents.kt, add @Serializable and @SerialName (TODO 1), create the shared Json (TODO 2), and write encodeEvents and decodeEvents (TODOs 3 and 4).
In Beans.kt, mark FeeService with @OpenForProxies (TODO 5), and PaymentEntity with @NoArgEntity and @OpenForProxies (TODO 6).

hints: encodeToString and decodeFromString are extension functions with reified types: json.encodeToString(events) and json.decodeFromString<List<PaymentEvent>>(text), or let the return type infer it.
The "type" field appears because the static type is List<PaymentEvent>, the sealed base. You don't configure it.
Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } covers both rules. Leave encodeDefaults alone: off is the default, and the test expects currency to be left out.
The marker annotations live in package workbench.kotlin: import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies and workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity.
lab.done: All seven tests in PluginsTest and EventsFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write a serializable refund hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a sealed RefundEvent with two subtypes, RefundRequested(refundId, amountMinor) and RefundSettled(refundId, settledAtEpochMs), serialized with the stable type names refund_requested and refund_settled, and a shared Json that tolerates new fields. Then write the Java version with Jackson annotations. Where does each version find the subtypes?

answer.html: @Serializable sealed interface RefundEvent { val refundId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("refund_requested") data class RefundRequested(override val refundId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : RefundEvent @Serializable @SerialName("refund_settled") data class RefundSettled(override val refundId: String, val settledAtEpochMs: Long) : RefundEvent // the plugin finds the subtypes at compile time, from the sealed hierarchy val refundJson = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }

alt.title: RefundEvent.java

recap: A compiler plugin changes what kotlinc emits, driven by annotations you configure. The annotations do nothing on their own.
all-open removes final from annotated classes and their members (not private members, not fields), so proxies can subclass them. kotlin-spring and kotlin-jpa are presets.
In Kotlin 2.4.21 the built-in quarkus preset knows only javax annotations: list the jakarta ones yourself.
no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor, hidden from Kotlin, callable from Java and reflection. It skips property initializers unless invokeInitializers is on.

kotlinx.serialization generates a $$serializer class at compile time. A sealed base gets a "type" discriminator: pin it with @SerialName, reuse one Json, and set ignoreUnknownKeys for evolving events.
KSP and kapt generate new source files. Prefer KSP; kapt runs Java processors on generated stubs and costs build time.

explain.prompt: A teammate's Quarkus 3 service has a Kotlin bean annotated @ApplicationScoped whose interceptor never fires, and the build uses the all-open quarkus preset. Explain what's going on in the class file and what you'd change.
explain.answer: Kotlin compiles classes and their methods as final unless something opens them. Interceptors in CDI work through generated subclasses that override the bean's methods, and a final class or method can't be overridden. The all-open plugin is supposed to remove final from classes with certain annotations, but it only does that for the annotations it's told about. The built-in quarkus preset in the Kotlin 2.4.21 plugin lists only the old javax.enterprise.context annotations, and Quarkus 3 uses jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped, so the preset doesn't match and the bean stays public final class. I'd configure all-open with the exact annotations the service uses, such as annotation("jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped") and annotation("jakarta.ws.rs.Path"), rebuild, and check one bean with javap to see that final is gone from the class and its public methods.

deeper.html:
The presets inside the 2.4.21 all-open plugin, read from the plugin's own classes, say more than the docs page. spring lists @Component, @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @SpringBootTest and also org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated, which the docs page leaves out. micronaut lists four AOP annotations, jpa lists Entity, Embeddable and MappedSuperclass in both namespaces, and quarkus lists only the two javax scopes. When a framework moves packages, presets lag behind, and listing annotations by name is the only setting you control.

On the command line the same plugins take -P options, which helps when you test a hypothesis with plain kotlinc: -Xplugin=<allopen jar> -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.allopen:annotation=com.example.OpenForProxies, and for no-arg -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.noarg:invokeInitializers=true. Maven users add <plugin>all-open</plugin> to the Kotlin Maven plugin with the kotlin-maven-allopen dependency. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, kotlin-maven-noarg also includes kotlin-maven-allopen.

kotlinx.serialization has more for event streams. Open polymorphism, where subclasses live in other modules, needs a SerializersModule that registers each one. classDiscriminator renames the "type" field if your schema already uses that name. coerceInputValues turns invalid values, such as an unknown enum constant, into the property's default instead of failing. And @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys (Experimental) relaxes unknown keys for one class instead of the whole Json instance.

Finally, the generated code is plain JVM bytecode, so it's fast and free of run-time reflection, which also makes it a good fit for GraalVM native images. The startup track covers why reflection is the hard part there.
